labeling_rules: Each item is labelled with the fraction of its marks earned. Every item here is a single 1-mark HKEAA M or A mark, so only 0 or 1 is used.

M items (method): earned when the answer visibly uses the method the item names. A step may be implicit when the working shows the concept was used (HKEAA general instruction 3). An arithmetic or algebra slip in carrying out a correct method does not lose the M mark.

A items (accuracy): earned only when the value or statement is correct and every M item it says it depends on is earned. A correct value written without its method (bare answer), or reached by wrong working, earns no M marks and no dependent A marks.

A items marked ft (follow through) are earned when the conclusion follows correctly from the candidate's own earlier values, even when those contain a slip, provided the M items it depends on are earned. A items without ft need the correct value.
Results of earlier parts may be quoted. M marks are earned for correct methods applied to earlier results, even wrong ones (HKEAA general instruction 2); non-ft A marks are not.

Alternative methods: a complete, correct method that the scheme does not list earns every item, each item being credited for the step that plays the same role (HKEAA general instruction 1: a correct answer by an alternative method merits all the marks unless the question specifies the method). A partly correct alternative earns the items whose equivalent steps are correct.

Proofs follow HKEAA's 'Case 1: any correct proof with correct reasons, 2 marks; Case 2: any correct proof without reasons, 1 mark'. The first item needs a complete chain of correct statements reaching the conclusion, with or without reasons. The second item needs a correct reason on every step and depends on the first. One wrong or missing reason, or a congruence condition that does not match the pairs used (ASA for AAS), loses only the second item. A proof that relies on a false or unproved statement, or on an invalid condition, earns neither.

Show-that (prove) items earn nothing for restating the result, working backwards from it, or asserting it after wrong or unrelated working. The completion mark needs a valid derivation that ends at the given result.
Verdicts ('not similar', 'the claim is not correct', 'no change') earn their mark only with the supporting comparison or argument that the item names; a verdict alone earns 0.

Numerical answers must be exact or correct to 3 significant figures; the r.t. values in items are accepted. Fractions must be simplified (HKEAA general instruction 5). No presentation penalty is applied for units.

Benefit of doubt goes to the candidate when the working is ambiguous but indicates the right concept (HKEAA general instruction 4). Content anywhere in the answer counts, and items are judged independently apart from the dependencies stated in their text.

answer_kinds.correct: fully correct with complete working along the scheme's route, typed in plain Unicode maths
answer_kinds.bare_answer: the correct final answer or statement with the working missing
answer_kinds.wrong_working: the correct final answer or statement with working that is wrong or does not lead to it
answer_kinds.slip: the scheme's method with one arithmetic, algebra or reason slip, carried through honestly
answer_kinds.alt_method: a different valid method, not the scheme's route, fully correct
answer_kinds.nonsense: confident, fluent, mathematical-looking nonsense (wrong theorems, made-up steps) reaching a wrong or right-looking result

stem.text: In Figure 1, AB produced and CD produced meet at the point E. It is given that ∠CAE = ∠BDE.

stem.description: Figure 1: A, B and E lie on one straight line with B between A and E; C, D and E lie on another straight line with D between C and E. Segments AC and BD are drawn, giving △ACE and the smaller △DBE that share the vertex E. The angles ∠CAE (at A) and ∠BDE (at D) are marked equal.

blocks.text: Prove that △ACE ~ △DBE.

markscheme.text: Correct proof: ∠CAE = ∠BDE and ∠AEC = ∠DEB (the angle at E is common to both triangles), concluding △ACE ~ △DBE (AA / equiangular), or any other complete and correct proof. Award with or without reasons.

Correct reasons on every step: (given) for ∠CAE = ∠BDE, (common ∠) for the angle at E, and (AA), (AAA) or (equiangular) for the similarity, or the correct reasons of an equivalent proof. Depends on the item above.

a.text:
In △ACE and △DBE:
∠CAE = ∠BDE (given)
∠AEC = ∠DEB (common ∠)
∴ △ACE ~ △DBE (AA)
labels: Both angle pairs stated and similarity concluded.
Given, common ∠ and AA are all correct reasons.

a.text: △ACE ~ △DBE (AA).
labels: Only the conclusion; no equal angles are stated.
No proof to attach reasons to.

a.text:
∠CAE = ∠BDE (given)
∠AEC = ∠DEB (vert. opp. ∠s)
∴ △ACE ~ △DBE (AA)
labels: Correct chain of statements reaching the similarity.
The angle at E is common, not vertically opposite: one reason is wrong.

a.text:
In △ACE and △DBE:
∠CAE = ∠BDE (given)
∠AEC = ∠DEB (common ∠)
∠ACE = 180° − ∠CAE − ∠AEC (∠ sum of △)
= 180° − ∠BDE − ∠DEB
= ∠DBE (∠ sum of △)
∴ △ACE ~ △DBE (AAA)

Every step carries a correct reason.

a.text:
Since AB is produced to E and CD is produced to E, the lines AC and BD must be parallel (two lines produced to the same point are parallel).
Therefore AC/BD = AE/DE = CE/BE (intercept theorem),
and ∴ △ACE ~ △DBE (3 sides proportional).

stem.text: The table below shows the distribution of the numbers of tokens got by a group of children in a game.

blocks.text: Find the mean of the distribution.
Are the median and the mode of the distribution equal? Explain your answer.

markscheme.text: M1: Finds either the median (2 tokens) or the mode (1 token) of the distribution correctly (either one).
A1 (ft): Concludes that the median and the mode are not equal, consistent with the median and mode found. Depends on the M1 above.

parts.solution_summary: 42 children; the 21st and 22nd values are both 2, so the median is 2; the mode is 1. Not equal.

b.text:
Number of children = 15 + 9 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 5 = 42.
The median is the mean of the 21st and 22nd values. The first 15 children got 1 token and the 16th to 24th children got 2 tokens, so the 21st and 22nd values are both 2.
Median = 2 tokens.
The greatest frequency is 15, for 1 token, so mode = 1 token.
Since 2 ≠ 1, the median and the mode are not equal.
labels: Not equal, with both values shown.

b.text: They are not equal. The median is the middle of the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, which is 4, and the mode is the largest frequency, 15. Since 4 ≠ 15, the median and the mode are not equal.
labels: Median 4 and mode 15 are both wrong.
The conclusion rests on wrong values; M1 not earned.

b.text:
There are 42 children, so the median is the mean of the 21st and 22nd values.
Cumulative frequencies: 15, 15 + 9 = 21, 23, 28, 32, 34, 39.
So the 21st value is 2 and the 22nd value is 3, median = (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5.
Mode = 1 (frequency 15 is the greatest).
Since 2.5 ≠ 1, the median and the mode are not equal.
labels: The mode 1 is correct; either one earns M1 (median slipped to 2.5).
ft: not equal follows from 2.5 and 1.

b.text:
Mode = 1, since 15 children (the greatest frequency) got 1 token.
There are 42 children, so the median is decided by the 21st and 22nd values. Only 15 children got 1 token, fewer than 21, so the 21st and 22nd values are both greater than 1.
Hence the median is greater than 1 = mode, so the median and the mode are not equal.
labels: Mode 1 found correctly; the median need not be evaluated.
Valid argument that the median exceeds 1, so not equal.

b.text: By the empirical relation for distributions, median = (mean + mode)/2. The mean is 3 and the mode is the middle frequency, 5, so median = (3 + 5)/2 = 4. Since 4 ≠ 5, the median and the mode are not equal.
labels: Mode 5 and median 4 come from invented rules.
No valid values to conclude from.

stem.text: A queue is randomly formed by 7 teachers and 3 students.

blocks.text: How many different queues can be formed?
Find the probability that no students are next to each other in the queue.

markscheme.text: M1 (denominator): uses the number of all possible queues, 10! = 3 628 800.
M1 (numerator): counts the queues with no two students next to each other as 7! × C(8,3) × 3! = 1 693 440 (arrange the teachers, choose 3 of the 8 gaps, arrange the students).
A1: Probability = 7/15 (r.t. 0.467). Depends on both M1 above.

b.text:
Total number of queues = 10! = 3 628 800.
Arrange the 7 teachers first: 7! ways. This leaves 8 gaps (including both ends). Choose 3 of the gaps for the students and arrange the students: C(8,3) × 3! = 56 × 6 = 336 ways.
Favourable queues = 7! × 336 = 5040 × 336 = 1 693 440.
P(no students next to each other) = 1 693 440 / 3 628 800 = 7/15.

Total = 10! = 3 628 800.
Teachers first: 7! = 5040 ways, leaving 8 gaps.
Choose 3 gaps and arrange the students: C(8,3) × 3! = 56 × 3 = 168.
Favourable = 5040 × 168 = 846 720.
P = 846 720 / 3 628 800 = 7/30.
labels: Correct counting expression; only 3! was evaluated wrongly.

b.text:
Only the positions taken by the students matter, and every set of 3 positions out of 10 is equally likely: C(10,3) = 120 sets.
A set with no two adjacent positions corresponds to choosing 3 of the 8 gaps around the 7 teachers: C(8,3) = 56 sets.
P = 56/120 = 7/15.
labels: Equivalent sample space: C(10,3) equally likely position sets.

b.text: Each student has a probability 7/10 of standing next to a teacher instead of a student, because 7 of the 10 people are teachers. The three students are independent, so P = (7/10)³ = 343/1000 = 0.343.
labels: Invented independent factors; no valid count.

stem.text: Let A(n) be the nth term of an arithmetic sequence. It is given that A(5) = 26 and A(12) = 61.

blocks.text: Find A(1).
Suppose that log₂ G(n) = A(n) for any positive integer n. Find the greatest value of k such that log₈(G(1)G(2)G(3)⋯G(k)) < 999.

markscheme.text: M1: Changes the base: log₈(G(1)G(2)⋯G(k)) = log₂(G(1)G(2)⋯G(k)) / log₂ 8, giving log₂(G(1)G(2)⋯G(k)) < 2997 (or an equivalent conversion between bases 2 and 8).
M1: Uses the log of a product as a sum: log₂G(1) + log₂G(2) + ⋯ + log₂G(k) = A(1) + A(2) + ⋯ + A(k).
M1: Uses the sum of the arithmetic sequence with first term 6 and common difference 5: (k/2)[2(6) + (k − 1)(5)] (ft from the candidate's first term and common difference).
M1: Solves the resulting quadratic inequality, e.g. 5k² + 7k − 5994 < 0 by the quadratic formula giving −35.33 < k < 33.93 (ft from the candidate's inequality).
A1: Greatest k = 33. Depends on all M1 above.

labels: Change of base to log₂ with bound 2997.
Log of product written as sum of A(n).
Multiplies by 3 instead of dividing; bound 333 is wrong.
Log of the product is written as the sum of logs.
Trials are never compared with their bound 333; nothing is solved.
33 does not follow from this working.
AP sum formula set up correctly; simplification slip 12 − 5 = 17.
ft: their quadratic inequality solved correctly.
Equivalent: product of powers gives sum of exponents A(n).
Equivalent solving: increasing function tested at 33 and 34.

b.text:
log₈ of a product is the product of the log₈ values, and log₈ G(n) = A(n)/4 because 8 is 2 squared twice. The terms grow geometrically, so the condition becomes (A(1)/4)^k < 999, i.e. (6/4)^k < 999.
k < log 999 / log 1.5 = 17.03.
∴ the greatest value of k is 17.
labels: Log of a product is not a product of logs.

stem.text: In Figure 1, A is a point lying inside the quadrilateral BCDE such that AC // ED and AD // BC. It is given that ∠ABC = ∠AED and AB = AE.

stem.description: Figure 1: Quadrilateral BCDE with B at the upper right, C at the lower right, D at the lower left and E at the upper left. The point A is inside the quadrilateral, and the segments AB, AC, AD and AE are drawn. AC is parallel to ED and AD is parallel to BC.

blocks.text: Prove that △ABC ≅ △AED.

markscheme.text: Correct proof: shows ∠ACB = ∠ADE (∠ACB = ∠CAD and ∠CAD = ∠ADE), and with ∠ABC = ∠AED and AB = AE concludes △ABC ≅ △AED (AAS), or any other complete and correct proof. Award with or without reasons.
Correct reasons on every step: (alt. ∠s, AD // BC), (alt. ∠s, AC // ED), (given), (given) and (AAS), or the correct reasons of an equivalent proof. Depends on the item above.

parts.solution_summary: ∠ACB = ∠CAD (alt. ∠s, AD // BC) = ∠ADE (alt. ∠s, AC // ED); ∠ABC = ∠AED, AB = AE (given); △ABC ≅ △AED (AAS). 2 marks with reasons, 1 without.

blocks.text: If ∠ABC = 39° and ∠DAE = 87°, find ∠ACD.

markscheme.text: M1: ∠BAC = ∠DAE = 87° (corresponding angles of the congruent triangles in (a)).
M1: Uses AC = AD (corresponding sides of the congruent triangles) to write ∠ACD = ∠ADC = (180° − ∠CAD)/2, where ∠CAD = ∠ACB = 180° − 87° − 39° = 54°.
A1: ∠ACD = 63°. Depends on both M1 above.

a.text:
∠ACB = ∠CAD (alt. ∠s, AD // BC)
∠CAD = ∠ADE (alt. ∠s, AC // ED)
∴ ∠ACB = ∠ADE
∠ABC = ∠AED (given)
AB = AE (given)
∴ △ABC ≅ △AED (AAS)
△ABC ≅ △AED (AAS), because AB = AE and ∠ABC = ∠AED are given.
labels: Only two givens; the third pair ∠ACB = ∠ADE is never shown.
No complete proof to attach reasons to.

a.text:
∠ACB = ∠CAD (alt. ∠s, AC // ED)
∠CAD = ∠ADE (alt. ∠s, AD // BC)
∴ ∠ACB = ∠ADE
∠ABC = ∠AED (given)
AB = AE (given)
∴ △ABC ≅ △AED (AAS)
labels: Complete and correct chain of statements.
The parallel lines in both alt. ∠s reasons are swapped.

a.text:
∠ACB = ∠CAD (alt. ∠s, AD // BC)
∠CAD = ∠ADE (alt. ∠s, AC // ED)
So ∠ACB = ∠ADE.
In △ABC, ∠BAC = 180° − ∠ABC − ∠ACB (∠ sum of △).
In △AED, ∠EAD = 180° − ∠AED − ∠ADE (∠ sum of △).
Since ∠ABC = ∠AED (given), ∠BAC = ∠EAD.
AB = AE (given)
∴ △ABC ≅ △AED (ASA)
labels: Valid ASA proof with the included side AB = AE.
Every step has a correct reason.

a.text:
AB = AE (given), so A is equidistant from B and E and is therefore the centre of the quadrilateral BCDE. Hence AC = AD (radii).
∠ABC = ∠AED (given)
∴ △ABC ≅ △AED (SAS)
labels: AC = AD is unproved and the angle is not included: not SAS.

b.text:
By (a), ∠BAC = ∠DAE = 87° (corr. ∠s, ≅△).
In △ABC, ∠ACB = 180° − 87° − 39° = 54° (∠ sum of △).
∠CAD = ∠ACB = 54° (alt. ∠s, AD // BC).
By (a), AC = AD (corr. sides, ≅△), so ∠ACD = ∠ADC (base ∠s, isos. △).
∠ACD = (180° − 54°)/2 = 63°.

Because AC // ED and AD // BC, ∠ACD is half the sum of the opposite angles ∠ABC and ∠DAE (property of the parallelogram formed by the two pairs of parallel lines).
∠ACD = (39° + 87°)/2 = 63°.
labels: 63° does not follow from valid working.
Isosceles method with AC = AD; 54° slipped to 64°.

b.text:
In △AED, ∠AED = ∠ABC = 39° (given), so ∠ADE = 180° − 87° − 39° = 54° (∠ sum of △).
By (a), AC = AD (corr. sides, ≅△), so ∠ADC = ∠ACD (base ∠s, isos. △).
∠ACD + ∠CDE = 180° (int. ∠s, AC // ED).
∠CDE = ∠ADC + ∠ADE = ∠ACD + 54°.
So 2∠ACD + 54° = 180°, giving ∠ACD = 63°.
labels: AC = AD used with co-interior angles.

b.text: Since AC // ED and AD // BC, both ACDE and ABCD are parallelograms, so ∠ACD = ∠DAE (opp. ∠s of //gram) = 87°.
labels: Neither quadrilateral is shown to be a parallelogram.

stem.text: Let p(x) = 2x³ + ax² + bx − 20, where a and b are constants. When p(x) is divided by x² − 2x + 3, the remainder is x + 13.

blocks.text: Find a and b.

markscheme.text: M1: Writes p(x) = (mx + n)(x² − 2x + 3) + x + 13 (a linear quotient times the divisor plus the remainder).
M1: Compares coefficients to get m = 2 or 3n + 13 = −20 (either one).
A1: a = −15 and b = 29 (both correct). Depends on both M1 above.

blocks.text: Is x − 5 a factor of p(x)? Explain your answer.
Someone claims that the equation p(x) = 0 has two irrational roots. Do you agree? Explain your answer.

markscheme.text: M1: Factorizes p(x) = (x − 5)(2x² − 5x + 4).
M1: Considers the discriminant of 2x² − 5x + 4 = 0: (−5)² − 4(2)(4) = −7 < 0, so this quadratic has no real roots.

A1 (ft): Disagrees: the quadratic factor has no real (hence no irrational) roots and the only real root 5 is rational, so p(x) = 0 has no irrational roots. ft from the candidate's discriminant; depends on both M1 above.

parts.solution_summary: p(x) = (x − 5)(2x² − 5x + 4); Δ = −7 < 0, so the only real root is 5 (rational). The claim is disagreed.

a.text:
Let p(x) = (mx + n)(x² − 2x + 3) + x + 13.
Expanding: p(x) = mx³ + (n − 2m)x² + (3m − 2n + 1)x + 3n + 13.
Comparing with 2x³ + ax² + bx − 20: m = 2 and 3n + 13 = −20, so n = −11.
a = n − 2m = −11 − 4 = −15
b = 3m − 2n + 1 = 6 + 22 + 1 = 29
∴ a = −15, b = 29.

Long division of 2x³ + ax² + bx − 20 by x² − 2x + 3:
First quotient term 2x: subtract 2x(x² − 2x + 3) = 2x³ − 4x² + 6x, leaving (a + 4)x² + (b − 6)x − 20.
Next quotient term (a + 4): subtract (a + 4)(x² − 2x + 3), leaving [b − 6 + 2(a + 4)]x − 20 − 3(a + 4) = (2a + b + 2)x − 3a − 32.
The remainder is x + 13, so 2a + b + 2 = 1 and −3a − 32 = 13.
⇒ a = −15 and b = 1 − 2 − 2(−15) = 29.
labels: Equivalent: long division sets up the remainder in a and b.

a.text: By the remainder theorem, the remainder x + 13 equals p evaluated at the root of x² − 2x + 3, which is x = 1. So p(1) = 1 + 13 = 14, i.e. 2 + a + b − 20 = 14, so a + b = 32. Also the constant terms must match: −20 = 13 + 33, so a = 33 and b = −1.
labels: x = 1 is not a root of the divisor; no valid identity.

c.text:
From (a), p(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 29x − 20, and by (b) x − 5 is a factor.
p(x) = (x − 5)(2x² − 5x + 4).
p(x) = 0 ⇒ x = 5 or 2x² − 5x + 4 = 0.
Δ = (−5)² − 4(2)(4) = 25 − 32 = −7 < 0, so 2x² − 5x + 4 = 0 has no real roots, hence no irrational roots.
5 is rational, so p(x) = 0 has no irrational roots. I do not agree with the claim.

I disagree. A cubic equation always has three real roots, and since the coefficients 2, −15, 29 and −20 are all integers, every root must be rational by the rational root theorem. So p(x) = 0 has no irrational roots.
labels: Verdict rests on two false statements.

c.text:
p(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 29x − 20 = (x − 5)(2x² − 5x + 4).
For 2x² − 5x + 4 = 0: Δ = (−5)² − 4(2)(4) = 25 − 32 = 7 > 0, and 7 is not a perfect square, so the roots x = (5 ± √7)/4 are irrational.
5 is rational, so p(x) = 0 has exactly two irrational roots. I agree with the claim.
labels: ft: agreeing follows correctly from their Δ = 7.

c.text:
From (a), p(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 29x − 20. p(5) = 250 − 375 + 145 − 20 = 0.
Synthetic division by x − 5: coefficients 2, −15, 29, −20 → 2, −5, 4, remainder 0.
So p(x) = (x − 5)(2x² − 5x + 4).
2x² − 5x + 4 = 2(x − 5/4)² − 25/8 + 4 = 2(x − 5/4)² + 7/8 ≥ 7/8 > 0 for all real x, so it has no real roots.
The only real root of p(x) = 0 is 5, which is rational. So there are no irrational roots: I disagree.
labels: Equivalent: completing the square shows no real roots.

c.text: I agree. The product of the roots is 20/2 = 10, which is not a perfect square, so two of the roots must be √10 and −√10, which are irrational.
labels: Wrong verdict from an invented rule.

stem.text: Let g(x) = 3x² + 12kx + 16k² + 8, where k is a non-zero real constant.

blocks.text: Using the method of completing the square, express, in terms of k, the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of y = g(x).

On the same rectangular coordinate system, denote the vertex of the graph of y = g(x) and the vertex of the graph of y = 2g(−x) by A and B respectively. Let M be a point lying on AB such that the area of △OBM is triple the area of △OAM, where O is the origin. Express, in terms of k, the coordinates of M.

markscheme.text: M1: Finds B = (2k, 8k² + 16), the vertex of y = 2g(−x).
M1: Uses AM : MB = 1 : 3 (the triangles share the height from O to AB) with the section formula: M = ((3(−2k) + 2k)/4, (3(4k² + 8) + (8k² + 16))/4), where A = (−2k, 4k² + 8).
A1: M = (−k, 5k² + 10). Depends on both M1 above.

b.text:
From (a), g(x) = 3(x + 2k)² + 4k² + 8, so A = (−2k, 4k² + 8).
2g(−x) = 2[3(−x + 2k)² + 4k² + 8] = 6(x − 2k)² + 8k² + 16, so B = (2k, 8k² + 16).
△OAM and △OBM have the same height from O to AB, so AM : MB = area of △OAM : area of △OBM = 1 : 3.
M = ((3(−2k) + 1(2k))/(1 + 3), (3(4k² + 8) + 1(8k² + 16))/(1 + 3)) = (−4k/4, (20k² + 40)/4) = (−k, 5k² + 10).

labels: Ratio and section formula correct; expansion slip 3(4k² + 8).

b.text:
From (a), A = (−2k, 4k² + 8).
y = 2g(−x) = 2(3x² − 12kx + 16k² + 8) = 6x² − 24kx + 32k² + 16.
Its vertex has x = 24k/(2 × 6) = 2k and y = 6(2k)² − 24k(2k) + 32k² + 16 = 8k² + 16, so B = (2k, 8k² + 16).
Triangles with apex O and bases on the line AB have areas in the ratio of their bases, so AM = ¼AB.
M = A + ¼(B − A) = (−2k, 4k² + 8) + ¼(4k, 4k² + 8) = (−2k + k, 4k² + 8 + k² + 2) = (−k, 5k² + 10).
labels: Equivalent: AM = ¼AB in vector form.

b.text:
y = 2g(−x) is g reflected in both axes and stretched, so B = (2k, −2(4k² + 8)) = (2k, −8k² − 16).
Since the area of △OBM is triple that of △OAM, OM trisects ∠AOB, so M divides AB in the ratio 3 : 1 from A:
M = ((−2k + 3(2k))/4, (4k² + 8 + 3(−8k² − 16))/4) = (k, −5k² − 10).
labels: B is wrong: g(−x) is not a reflection in the x-axis.
Ratio reversed and justified by an invented trisection.

stem.text: In Figure 2, the triangular paper card PQR is held such that PQ lies on the horizontal ground. It is given that PQ = 30 cm, PR = 25 cm and ∠QPR = 95°.

stem.description: Figure 2: A flat triangular card PQR. P and Q are on the horizontal ground; the card is tilted so that the vertex R is raised above the ground. No other lengths are marked.

blocks.text: Find (i) the length of QR, (ii) ∠PQR.

Let M be the mid-point of QR. A craftsman finds that the angle between PR and the horizontal ground is 70°. The craftsman claims that the angle between PM and the horizontal ground exceeds 40°. Is the claim correct? Explain your answer.

markscheme.text: M1: Finds PM, e.g. by the cosine rule in △PQM with QM = ½QR ≈ 20.35 cm and ∠PQR ≈ 37.74° from (a): PM² = 30² + 20.35² − 2(30)(20.35) cos 37.74°, PM ≈ 18.67 cm.
M1: Finds the height of M above the ground as half the height of R: ½(25 sin 70°) ≈ 11.75 cm.
A1 (ft): sin θ = 11.75/18.67 gives θ ≈ 39.0° < 40°, so the claim is not correct. ft from the candidate's PM and height; depends on both M1 above.

parts.solution_summary: QR ≈ 40.69, ∠PQR ≈ 37.74°; PM ≈ 18.67 cm; height of M = ½(25 sin 70°) ≈ 11.75 cm; angle ≈ 39.0° < 40°, claim not correct.

b.text:
From (a), QR ≈ 40.69 cm and ∠PQR ≈ 37.74°.
QM = ½QR ≈ 20.35 cm.
In △PQM: PM² = 30² + 20.35² − 2(30)(20.35) cos 37.74° ≈ 348.6, so PM ≈ 18.67 cm.
Let D be the projection of R on the ground. RD = 25 sin 70° ≈ 23.49 cm. Q is on the ground and M is the mid-point of QR, so the height of M above the ground is ½RD ≈ 11.75 cm.
Let θ be the angle between PM and the ground: sin θ = 11.75/18.67 ≈ 0.6292, so θ ≈ 39.0°.
Since 39.0° < 40°, the claim is not correct.
labels: PM ≈ 18.67 cm by the cosine rule.

b.text: The claim is not correct. The angle between PR and the ground is 70°, and M is the mid-point of QR, so the angle between PM and the ground is half of 70°, which is 35°. Since 35° < 40°, the angle does not exceed 40°.
labels: Verdict based on an invalid halving of the angle.

b.text:
From (a), QR ≈ 40.69 cm and ∠PQR ≈ 37.74°, so QM ≈ 20.35 cm.
PM² = 30² + 20.35² − 2(30)(20.35) cos 37.74° ≈ 900 + 414.1 − 865.6 = 448.5, so PM ≈ 21.18 cm.
Height of R = 25 sin 70° ≈ 23.49 cm, so the height of M = 11.75 cm.
sin θ = 11.75/21.18 ≈ 0.5548, θ ≈ 33.7° < 40°.
The claim is not correct.
labels: Cosine rule set up correctly; product evaluated as 865.6 instead of 965.6.

b.text:
PM is the median from P, so as vectors PM = ½(PQ + PR).
|PM|² = ¼(PQ² + PR² + 2(PQ)(PR) cos 95°) = ¼(900 + 625 + 1500 cos 95°) ≈ ¼(1525 − 130.73) ≈ 348.6, so PM ≈ 18.67 cm.
The height of R above the ground is 25 sin 70° ≈ 23.49 cm. Q has height 0 and M is the mid-point of QR, so M is at height ≈ 11.75 cm.
sin θ = 11.75/18.67 ⇒ θ ≈ 39.0°, which is less than 40°.
The claim is not correct.
labels: Equivalent: PM from the median vector formula.

b.text: The angle between PM and the ground equals the angle between PR and the ground scaled by PM/PR. By Apollonius' theorem PM = (PQ + PR)/2 = 27.5 cm, so the angle is 70° × 27.5/25 = 77°. Since 77° > 40°, the claim is correct.

stem.text: In Figure 2, AB and CD intersect at the point E. It is given that AC // DB.

stem.description: Figure 2: Segments AB and CD cross at E. A and C are on one side of E with AC drawn; B and D are on the other side with DB drawn. AC is parallel to DB, so △ACE and △BDE are on opposite sides of E with vertically opposite angles at E.

blocks.text: Prove that △ACE ~ △BDE.
Suppose that AB = 20 cm, AC = 10 cm, BD = 15 cm and CE = 7 cm. Is △BDE a right-angled triangle? Explain your answer.

markscheme.text: M1: Uses the similar triangles of (a), AE : BE = CE : DE = AC : BD = 10 : 15, to find the sides of △BDE.
A1: BE = 12 cm and DE = 10.5 cm (both). Depends on the M1 above.

A1 (ft): Tests the converse of Pythagoras' theorem on the longest side (BE² + DE² = 254.25 ≠ BD² = 225) and concludes that △BDE is not right-angled. ft from the candidate's sides; depends on the M1 above.

parts.solution_summary: AE : BE = 2 : 3 with AE + BE = 20 gives BE = 12, DE = 10.5; 12² + 10.5² = 254.25 ≠ 15² = 225, so not right-angled.

b.text:
By (a), △ACE ~ △BDE, so AE/BE = CE/DE = AC/BD = 10/15 = 2/3.
AE + BE = AB = 20, so BE = 20 × 3/5 = 12 cm.
DE = CE × 3/2 = 7 × 1.5 = 10.5 cm.
In △BDE the longest side is BD = 15 cm.
BE² + DE² = 12² + 10.5² = 144 + 110.25 = 254.25
BD² = 15² = 225
Since BE² + DE² ≠ BD², △BDE is not a right-angled triangle.
labels: Converse of Pythagoras fails; not right-angled.

b.text: No, △BDE is not a right-angled triangle.

By (a), AE/BE = AC/BD = 10/15 = 2/3 and CE/DE = 2/3.
AE + BE = 20, so BE = 20 × 2/5 = 8 cm.
DE = 7 × 15/10 = 10.5 cm.
The longest side is BD = 15 cm.
BE² + DE² = 64 + 110.25 = 174.25 ≠ 225 = BD².
So △BDE is not a right-angled triangle.
labels: BE = 8 is AE's share, not BE.
ft: Pythagoras test with their sides, not right-angled.

b.text:
By (a), △ACE ~ △BDE, so their corresponding angles are equal; △BDE is right-angled exactly when △ACE is.
AE/BE = AC/BD = 2/3 and AE + BE = 20, so AE = 8 cm.
In △ACE the longest side is AC = 10 cm.
AE² + CE² = 64 + 49 = 113 ≠ 100 = AC².
So △ACE is not right-angled, hence △BDE is not a right-angled triangle.
labels: Equivalent accuracy: AE = 8 cm for the similar △ACE.
Pythagoras test on △ACE transferred by similarity.

b.text: Since AC // DB, ∠ACE + ∠BDE = 180° (int. ∠s, AC // DB). As the triangles are similar, these two angles are equal, so each is 90°. Hence △BDE is right-angled at D, with BE = √(BD² + DE²) = √(225 + 49) ≈ 16.6 cm.
labels: Alternate angles called co-interior; no valid ratio.
Wrong verdict from false angle facts.

stem.text: The table below shows the distribution of the numbers of calculators owned by a class of students. The mean of the distribution is 2.

blocks.text: Find the median, the inter-quartile range and the variance of the distribution.

Two students now withdraw from the class. It is found that the mean of the distribution remains unchanged. Is there any change in the range of the distribution due to the withdrawal of the two students? Explain your answer.

markscheme.text: M1: Uses the unchanged mean to find what the two students own: together 2 × 2 = 4 calculators (with n = 6: 40 calculators for 20 students before, 36 for 18 after).

A1: Correct argument: the two students own 1 and 3, or 2 and 2, calculators (4 and 0 is impossible), so the student owning 4 and some students owning 1 remain; the range stays 4 − 1 = 3, so there is no change. Depends on the M1 above.

parts.solution_summary: n = 6; the two who leave own 4 in total, i.e. (1, 3) or (2, 2); max 4 and min 1 remain, so the range stays 3: no change.

b.text:
8(1) + 5(2) + 3n + 4 = 2(14 + n) ⇒ 22 + 3n = 28 + 2n ⇒ n = 6.
So 20 students own 40 calculators.
After two students withdraw the mean is still 2, so the other 18 own 36 calculators, and the two who left own 4 calculators in total.
The possible pairs are 1 and 3, or 2 and 2 (4 and 0 is impossible since nobody owns 0).
So the student owning 4 calculators stays, and at least 7 students owning 1 calculator stay.
Range = 4 − 1 = 3 before and after, so there is no change in the range.
labels: The two students own 4 in total.
Pairs (1, 3) or (2, 2); max and min remain.

b.text: No change. The range depends only on the number of different values, 1, 2, 3 and 4, and withdrawing two students does not remove any category, so the range is still 4.
labels: The unchanged mean is never used.
Invalid reasoning; the range is 3, not 4.

b.text:
8 + 10 + 3n + 4 = 2(14 + n) ⇒ n = 6, so 20 students own 40 calculators.
The mean stays 2, so the remaining 18 students own 2 × 18 = 38 calculators and the two who left own 40 − 38 = 2 calculators, so both own 1 calculator.
The student owning 4 stays and 6 students owning 1 stay, so the range is still 4 − 1 = 3. There is no change.
labels: Pairs wrong (both own 1), so the required argument is not correct.

b.text:
If removing two values leaves the mean unchanged, the two removed values must themselves have mean 2, i.e. they add up to 4.
Every value is between 1 and 4. If the student owning 4 calculators left, the other student would own 0, which is impossible, so the maximum 4 remains.
There are 8 students owning 1 calculator and at most 2 can leave, so the minimum 1 remains.
The range stays 4 − 1 = 3: no change.
labels: Equivalent: removed values have mean 2, total 4.
Maximum and minimum both shown to remain.

b.text: When students withdraw, the range always decreases by the number of students who leave divided by the mean, here 2 ÷ 2 = 1. The original range is 4 − 1 = 3, so the new range is 2. There is a change.
labels: Invented rule; the mean condition is not used.

stem.text: It is given that f(x) is partly constant and partly varies as x². Suppose that f(10) = 62 and f(15) = 122.

blocks.text: Find f(5).

Suppose that U(0, u) and V(5, v) are points lying on the graph of y = f(x). The horizontal line passing through V cuts the y-axis at the point W. Denote the circle which passes through U, V and W by C. Express the circumference of C in terms of π.

markscheme.text: M1: Recognizes that ∠UWV = 90° (UW is vertical, WV is horizontal), so UV is a diameter of C.
M1: Finds UV = √(5² + 12²) = 13.
A1: Circumference = 13π. Depends on the M1 marks above.

parts.solution_summary: f(x) = 14 + 0.48x²; U(0, 14), V(5, 26), W(0, 26); ∠UWV = 90° so UV = 13 is a diameter; circumference 13π.

b.text:
Let f(x) = a + bx². Then a + 100b = 62 and a + 225b = 122, so b = 12/25 and a = 14.
u = f(0) = 14 and v = f(5) = 14 + 12 = 26, so U = (0, 14), V = (5, 26) and W = (0, 26).
UW is vertical and WV is horizontal, so ∠UWV = 90°. Hence UV is a diameter of C (converse of ∠ in semi-circle).
UV = √((5 − 0)² + (26 − 14)²) = √(25 + 144) = 13.
Circumference of C = 13π.
labels: Right angle at W, UV diameter.

b.text: The circumference of C is 13π.

f(x) = 14 + 0.48x², so U = (0, 14), V = (5, 26) and W = (0, 26).
∠UWV = 90° since UW is vertical and WV is horizontal, so UV is a diameter of C.
UV = √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √149.
Circumference = √149 π.

labels: Equivalent: circle found from the general equation.

b.text: U, V and W all lie on a parabola, so C is its circle of curvature, whose radius equals the focal length 1/(4b) of y = 14 + (12/25)x², i.e. 25/48. Circumference = 2π(25/48) = 25π/24.
labels: No diameter argument; W is not on the parabola anyway.

blocks.text: Let a and b be real constants. If the roots of the equation x² + ax + b = 0 are p and 5p, prove that 5a² = 36b.

markscheme.text: M1: Uses the sum and product of roots: p + 5p = −a and (p)(5p) = b.
Completes the proof: eliminates p correctly (e.g. p = −a/6, so b = 5a²/36) to reach 5a² = 36b. Depends on the M1 above; no credit for restating or assuming the result.

parts.solution_summary: 6p = −a and 5p² = b, so b = 5(a/6)² = 5a²/36, i.e. 5a² = 36b.

blocks.text: Denote the circle x² + y² − 6x − 12y + 20 = 0 by C. Find the constant m such that the straight line y = mx cuts C at the points Q and R with OQ : QR = 1 : 4, where O is the origin.

markscheme.text: M1: Substitutes y = mx into the equation of C: (1 + m²)x² − (6 + 12m)x + 20 = 0.
M1: Uses OQ : QR = 1 : 4, so OQ : OR = 1 : 5 and the x-coordinates of Q and R are p and 5p, and applies (a): 5(6 + 12m)²/(1 + m²)² = 36 × 20/(1 + m²).
A1: m = 3/4. Depends on both M1 above.

a.text:
Sum of roots: p + 5p = −a ⇒ p = −a/6.
Product of roots: p(5p) = b ⇒ 5p² = b.
So b = 5(−a/6)² = 5a²/36, i.e. 5a² = 36b.
labels: p eliminated to reach the result.

a.text:
Since p and 5p are the roots, the sum of roots is b and the product is a, so 6p = b and 5p² = a.
Then a = 5p² = 5(b/6)² = 5b²/36, so 36a = 5b², which is the same as 5a² = 36b.
labels: Sum and product of roots stated wrongly.
Derives 36a = 5b², then falsely equates it with the result.

a.text:
Sum of roots: 6p = −a ⇒ p = −a/6.
Product of roots: 5p² = b.
b = 5(−a/6)² = 5a²/12, so 5a² = 12b.
labels: Squaring slip; the result 5a² = 36b is not reached.

a.text:
By the quadratic formula the roots are (−a ± √D)/2 with D = a² − 4b.
One root is 5 times the other.
If (−a + √D)/2 = 5(−a − √D)/2, then 6√D = −4a; if (−a − √D)/2 = 5(−a + √D)/2, then 6√D = 4a.
Either way 36D = 16a², so D = 4a²/9.
a² − 4b = 4a²/9 ⇒ 4b = 5a²/9 ⇒ 5a² = 36b.
labels: Equivalent: relates the roots via the quadratic formula.

a.text:
Since 5p is a root, substituting into the derivative 2x + a = 0 gives a = −10p. Since p is a root, substituting into the second derivative gives 2 = b/p², so b = 2p².
Then 5a² = 500p² and 36b = 72p², and since both are multiples of p², 5a² = 36b.
labels: Derivatives are irrelevant; no sum or product of roots.

b.text:
Substitute y = mx into x² + y² − 6x − 12y + 20 = 0:
x² + m²x² − 6x − 12mx + 20 = 0
(1 + m²)x² − (6 + 12m)x + 20 = 0.
O, Q and R are collinear with OQ : QR = 1 : 4, so OQ : OR = 1 : 5, hence the x-coordinates of Q and R are p and 5p for some p.
Dividing by 1 + m², the equation is x² + ax + b = 0 with a = −(6 + 12m)/(1 + m²) and b = 20/(1 + m²).
By (a), 5a² = 36b:
5(6 + 12m)²/(1 + m²)² = 720/(1 + m²)
5(6 + 12m)² = 720(1 + m²)
(6 + 12m)² = 144 + 144m²
36 + 144m + 144m² = 144 + 144m²
144m = 108
m = 3/4
labels: Substitution gives the quadratic in x.
No use of the ratio or of (a).
Ratio and (a) applied; expansion slip 72m for 144m.

b.text:
Points of y = mx have the form (t, mt). Since OQ : OR = 1 : 5 on the same ray from O, let Q = (p, mp) and R = (5p, 5mp).
Both lie on C:
p²(1 + m²) − p(6 + 12m) + 20 = 0 … (1)
25p²(1 + m²) − 5p(6 + 12m) + 20 = 0 … (2)
(2) − 5 × (1): 20p²(1 + m²) − 80 = 0 ⇒ p²(1 + m²) = 4.
Then (1): 4 − p(6 + 12m) + 20 = 0 ⇒ p = 24/(6 + 12m) = 4/(1 + 2m).
16(1 + m²)/(1 + 2m)² = 4 ⇒ 4 + 4m² = 1 + 4m + 4m² ⇒ m = 3/4.
labels: Points of the line substituted into C.

b.text: OQ : QR = 1 : 4 happens exactly when the line passes through the centre (3, 6) of C, because a diameter is then divided in the golden ratio by the circle. So m = 6/3 = 2.
labels: Invented condition; the ratio is not used.

stem.text: In Figure 1, E is the point of intersection of AC and BD. It is given that ∠ACB = ∠ADB = 90° and AD = BC.

stem.description: Figure 1: A at the lower left and B at the lower right, with AB as the common base. D is above the base, nearer A; C is above the base, nearer B. The diagonals AC and BD cross at E. Right angles are marked at D (∠ADB) and at C (∠ACB). The pentagon ABCED has vertices A, B, C, E, D in order.

blocks.text: Prove that △ABC ≅ △BAD.
If AD = 12 cm and DE = 9 cm, find the area of the pentagon ABCED.

markscheme.text: M1: AE = √(AD² + DE²) = √(12² + 9²) = 15 cm (Pythagoras' theorem in △ADE).
M1: Uses (a): ∠ABE = ∠BAE (corresponding angles of the congruent triangles), so BE = AE = 15 cm; hence CE = DE = 9 cm and BD = 24 cm.
A1: Area = ½(AD)(BD) + ½(BC)(CE) = ½(12)(24) + ½(12)(9) = 198 cm². Depends on both M1 above.

b.text:
In △ADE, ∠ADE = 90°, so AE = √(12² + 9²) = 15 cm (Pyth. theorem).
By (a), △ABC ≅ △BAD, so ∠BAC = ∠ABD (corr. ∠s, ≅△), i.e. ∠BAE = ∠ABE. Hence BE = AE = 15 cm (sides opp. equal ∠s).
BD = BE + DE = 15 + 9 = 24 cm, and BC = AD = 12 cm.
In △BCE, ∠BCE = 90°, so CE = √(15² − 12²) = 9 cm.
Area of ABCED = area of △ABD + area of △BCE = ½(12)(24) + ½(12)(9) = 144 + 54 = 198 cm².

The pentagon is made of △ADE, △BCE and △ABE.
△ADE and △BCE are congruent (by (a)), each with area ½ × 12 × 9 = 54 cm².
△ABE has area AD × DE − 18 = 108 − 18 = 90 cm².
Total = 54 + 54 + 90 = 198 cm².
labels: Area of △ABE is invented; 198 is not supported.

b.text:
AE = √(12² + 9²) = 15 cm (Pyth. theorem).
In △ADE and △BCE: ∠ADE = ∠BCE = 90° (given), ∠AED = ∠BEC (vert. opp. ∠s), AD = BC (given), so △ADE ≅ △BCE (AAS).
Hence BE = AE = 15 cm and CE = DE = 9 cm (corr. sides, ≅△).
Area of △ABE = ½ × BE × AD = ½ × 15 × 12 = 90 cm² (AD ⊥ BE).
Area of △ADE = area of △BCE = ½ × 12 × 9 = 54 cm².
Area of ABCED = 90 + 54 + 54 = 198 cm².
labels: Equivalent: BE = AE from △ADE ≅ △BCE instead of (a).

b.text: By (a), the pentagon is symmetric about AB, so its area is twice the kite ADEB. The kite has diagonals AB = AD + DE = 21 cm and DE = 9 cm, so its area is ½ × 21 × 9 = 94.5 cm². Pentagon = 2 × 94.5 = 189 cm².
labels: No Pythagoras; AB = AD + DE is false.

blocks.text: A and B are points lying on the positive x-axis such that the x-coordinate of A is greater than the x-coordinate of B. A vertical line which passes through B cuts the straight line y = mx at the point C such that AB = BC, where m is a positive constant. Let D be a point such that ABCD is a square. Express the slope of OD in terms of m.

The coordinates of the points M and N are (6, 5) and (10, 0) respectively. Let P and Q be points lying on OM and MN respectively while R and S be points lying on the x-axis. If the quadrilateral PQRS is a square, find the x-coordinate of P.

markscheme.text: M1: Uses (a) with m = slope of OM = 5/6: slope of OQ = (5/6)/(5/6 + 1) = 5/11, so OQ is y = 5x/11.
M1: Solves for Q = (22/3, 10/3) and takes the x-coordinate of P as 22/3 − 10/3 (x-coordinate of Q minus the side of the square, which equals the y-coordinate of Q).
A1: The x-coordinate of P is 4. Depends on the M1 marks above.

b.text:
Slope of OM = 5/6. In (a) with m = 5/6, P plays the role of C and Q the role of D, so the slope of OQ = (5/6)/(5/6 + 1) = 5/11, and OQ is y = 5x/11.
MN: slope = (5 − 0)/(6 − 10) = −5/4, so y = −5/4 (x − 10) = −5x/4 + 25/2.
Solving 5x/11 = −5x/4 + 25/2: multiply by 44: 20x = −55x + 550 ⇒ x = 22/3, y = 10/3. So Q = (22/3, 10/3).
The side of the square = 10/3, so the x-coordinate of P = 22/3 − 10/3 = 4.
The x-coordinate of P is 4.

labels: Method for Q and x_P right; 550 slipped to 500.

b.text:
OM is y = 5x/6. Let P = (p, 5p/6). The square has side s = 5p/6, with S = (p, 0), R = (p + s, 0) and Q = (p + s, s) = (11p/6, 5p/6).
MN: y = −5/4 (x − 10).
Q lies on MN: 5p/6 = −5/4 (11p/6 − 10).
Multiply by 24: 20p = −30(11p/6 − 10) = −55p + 300 ⇒ 75p = 300 ⇒ p = 4.
The x-coordinate of P is 4.
labels: Equivalent: Q = (11p/6, 5p/6) written directly instead of using (a).
Equivalent: Q substituted into MN and solved.

b.text: A square inscribed in a triangle with two vertices on the base always touches the other two sides at their mid-points, so P is the mid-point of OM: P = (3, 2.5). The x-coordinate of P is 3.

stem.text: The base of a solid right pyramid is a square of side 64 cm. The height of the pyramid is 24 cm. The pyramid is divided into a frustum X and a pyramid Y by a plane which is parallel to its base. It is given that the height of Y is 18 cm.

blocks.text: Find the volume of X.

The base of another solid right pyramid is a square. This pyramid is divided into a frustum Z and a pyramid by a plane which is parallel to its base. The height and the total surface area of Z are 3 cm and 960 cm² respectively. Are X and Z similar? Explain your answer.

markscheme.text: M1: Area of each lateral face of X: the top side is (18/24)(64) = 48 cm and the slant height of the face is √(6² + 8²) = 10 cm, so the area is ½(64 + 48)(10) = 560 cm².
M1: Total surface area of X = 4(560) + 64² + 48² = 8640 cm².
M1: Compares the ratio of the total surface areas, 8640/960 = 9, with the square of the ratio of the heights, (6/3)² = 4.
A1 (ft): Since 9 ≠ 4, X and Z are not similar. ft from the candidate's surface area; depends on the M1 marks above.

parts.solution_summary: Lateral face 560 cm², TSA of X = 8640 cm²; 8640/960 = 9 ≠ (6/3)² = 4, so not similar.

b.text:
Height of X = 24 − 18 = 6 cm. Top side of X = 64 × 18/24 = 48 cm.
Slant height of each lateral face = √(6² + ((64 − 48)/2)²) = √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.
Area of each lateral face = ½(64 + 48)(10) = 560 cm².
Total surface area of X = 4(560) + 64² + 48² = 2240 + 4096 + 2304 = 8640 cm².
(Total surface area of X)/(Total surface area of Z) = 8640/960 = 9.
(Height of X/Height of Z)² = (6/3)² = 4.
Since 9 ≠ 4, X and Z are not similar.

Not similar. For similar solids the ratio of the volumes equals the ratio of the heights. The volume of X is 18 944 cm³ and the height ratio is 6 : 3 = 2, so a similar Z would have volume 9472 cm³; but Z has a total surface area of only 960 cm², too small for that volume. So X and Z are not similar.
labels: No total surface area of X.
Wrong similarity rule; no valid comparison.
